accroche: In 1986, a Swiss journalist found the caves of a people presented fifteen years earlier as frozen in the Stone Age empty.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1971, Manuel Elizalde, the Philippine government's head of national minorities, announced the discovery of a group of twenty-six people in the tropical forest of Mindanao: the Tasaday. According to the reports of the time, they had no pottery, cloth, metal, houses, weapons, dogs, or cultivated plants, and lived dressed in leaves, eating what they gathered, with no knowledge of the outside world. The story made the cover of National Geographic in 1972 and the subject of a bestselling book, The Gentle Tasaday, published by the journalist John Nance in 1975. About a dozen scientists invited by PANAMIN, Elizalde's agency, visited the site in 1972 and 1973; in 1974, all contact was cut off. For thirteen years a blanket of silence fell over the Tasaday, and independent researchers and reporters were forbidden to go there.

## The Empty Caves

A month after the fall of President Ferdinand Marcos, in March 1986, the Swiss journalist Oswald Iten took advantage of the political chaos to travel to the site without authorization. He reported the caves deserted and found the Tasaday living in houses, dressed normally. A week later, the German magazine Stern photographed the same man Iten had, this time dressed in leaves, cloth underwear showing beneath. Hundreds of articles then took up the affair as proof of a complete fabrication, blamed on Elizalde and his agency.

## Neither a Pure Hoax, Nor the Stone Age

The reality, established later through collective research, is less settled than either of the two versions that followed one another. In 1992, the American Anthropological Association published The Tasaday Controversy: Assessing the Evidence, a collective volume edited by the anthropologist Thomas Headland that brings together the arguments of both camps. The Encyclopedia.com overview, drawing on that volume, concludes that neither extreme reading holds up. By the early 1990s, no specialist claimed any longer that the Tasaday lived in the Stone Age; but none claimed either that they never existed. It lists eight facts that no anthropologist disputes, among them these: the Tasaday already possessed trade goods and wore commercial cloth in 1971, and the stone tools displayed in Manila and photographed were not genuine: they had been made at the request of PANAMIN staff, for press correspondents.

What the episode demonstrates, then, is not that a people was invented out of whole cloth, but that a real people, small in number and trading with its farming neighbors, was staged to resemble a visitor's idea of prehistory. The underwear showing beneath the leaves is not proof that nothing existed: it is proof that leaves had been added to someone who did exist, and who was already wearing commercial cloth in 1971.

repere.texte: According to the Encyclopedia.com overview, drawing on Thomas Headland's edited volume, eight facts are disputed by no anthropologist, including the presence of commercial cloth among the Tasaday as early as 1971.

carte.punch: Photographed in leaves by a German magazine, the man was wearing cloth underwear, visible beneath.
carte.idee: In 1971, the Philippine government announced the discovery of a people frozen in the Stone Age, the Tasaday. In 1986, a journalist found their caves empty. Neither the original story nor the total-hoax version holds up: the people existed, but their “prehistory” had been staged.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: An overview of the controversy, from the 1971 announcement to later linguistic and ethnographic studies.

quiz.question: What does the Encyclopedia.com overview, drawing on the collective volume Thomas Headland edited in 1992, conclude after weighing the arguments of both camps?
choix: That the Tasaday undoubtedly lived in the Stone Age
That neither extreme account, an untouched people or a total hoax, holds up
That the Tasaday never existed and the whole case was invented by the press
That the affair can never be settled, for lack of any admissible evidence
quiz.explication: The overview lists facts no anthropologist disputes: the group existed, but its staging as a “Stone Age people” (displayed tools made on request, cloth already present, trade with neighbors) does not hold up. Neither extreme account therefore survives examination.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who announces the discovery of the Tasaday in 1971, and under what authority?
choix: The journalist John Nance, on behalf of National Geographic
Manuel Elizalde, head of PANAMIN, the Philippine agency in charge of national minorities
The Swiss journalist Oswald Iten, on an independent assignment
President Ferdinand Marcos, at an official press conference
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Manuel Elizalde, head of PANAMIN (Presidential Assistant on National Minorities), who announces the discovery in 1971 and whose agency, together with the Marcos government, then forbids independent researchers and reporters to visit the site.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Swiss journalist Oswald Iten observe in March 1986, a month after the fall of Ferdinand Marcos?
choix: Deserted caves, with the Tasaday living in houses, dressed normally
A military camp installed exactly where the caves had been
The Tasaday still dressed in leaves and living exactly as in 1971
No trace of human presence anywhere on the site
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Taking advantage of the political chaos following Marcos's fall, Iten travels to the site without authorization and reports the caves empty: the Tasaday are living in houses and wearing ordinary clothes, not the leaves of the early reports.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Encyclopedia.com overview say about the stone tools displayed in Manila and photographed after the 1971 discovery?
choix: They were inherited over generations and knapped with Upper Paleolithic sophistication
They were not genuine: they had been made at the request of PANAMIN staff, for journalists
They were knapped by National Geographic reporters during filming
No stone tools were ever displayed or photographed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Among the eight undisputed facts, the stone tools displayed in Manila and photographed had been made at the request of PANAMIN staff, for newspaper correspondents: they were not genuine Tasaday tools, and the group did not use stone as Upper Paleolithic humans did.
